summaries.example: Imagine a class history book that names many famous thinkers but leaves out every woman who had important ideas. A feminist historian might look for those missing thinkers, ask why they were left out, and add their work to the story. They might also check whether the book describes women as less clever or less able than men.
summaries.summary: Feminist history of philosophy asks how the usual story of philosophy was built and whether it left out women or treated them unfairly. Feminist philosophers study statements by famous thinkers that say women are weaker or less rational. They also look more closely at ideas that seem universal, such as reason and objectivity, to see whether those ideas were linked with men in hidden ways. Another important task is finding women philosophers and showing what they contributed. Adding names is not always enough; teachers and historians must find a meaningful place for their ideas in the whole story. Feminist philosophers do not all agree. Some mainly criticize the old canon, while others find helpful ideas in thinkers they also criticize. The entry presents this work as a project of recognition: noticing people, writings, questions, and ways of thinking that earlier histories often failed to recognize.
key_ideas: Some women philosophers were left out of many traditional histories of philosophy.
Some famous philosophers wrote ideas that described women as inferior or connected good thinking with being male.
Feminist philosophers reread old works, question unfair ideas, and recover women thinkers.
Different feminist readers may find both problems and useful ideas in the same philosopher.
The larger goal is to make the story of philosophy more accurate and welcoming.
summaries.why_it_matters: History affects what people think philosophy is and who seems able to do it. If students see only men in the story, they may wrongly believe that women never had important ideas. Studying the history more carefully can correct that picture and encourage a fuller understanding of philosophy. It also teaches us to ask whether supposedly neutral ideas were shaped by unfair assumptions.

important_terms.definition: A group of works and thinkers that a field treats as especially important and teaches often.
A careful look at the past that asks who was included, who was left out, and why.
An unfair belief or treatment based on someone being a woman or on ideas about women.
Giving something or someone proper attention, respect, or a place in a shared story.

questions_to_think_about: Who gets called an important thinker in the books you read?
Can an old book contain both unfair ideas and useful ideas?
What should teachers do when they discover a thinker who was left out?
How might a story change when new people are added?

summaries.example: Suppose a syllabus presents Aristotle as a major thinker but treats his comments about women as irrelevant mistakes. One feminist approach would record and criticize those comments. Another would ask whether his larger theory of form and matter uses a hierarchy that is connected to male and female symbolism, making the bias part of the theory rather than an easily removable opinion. A different feminist reader might still find value in parts of Aristotle’s ethical theory, such as its attention to emotion, care, and concrete circumstances. These approaches need not produce one final interpretation.
summaries.summary: The entry examines feminist engagement with the European philosophical canon through criticism, revision, and appropriation. Feminist critics first catalog explicit claims that women are inferior. They then investigate whether apparently universal concepts—especially reason, objectivity, form, and matter—carry gendered meanings. A further, synoptic approach interprets the tradition more broadly, arguing that its ideals of rationality and objectivity have often been symbolically associated with the masculine. The entry distinguishes historical gendering from the stronger claim that a concept is inherently gender-biased; even the stronger claim would support rethinking a concept rather than automatically abandoning reason or objectivity. Feminist historians also recover women philosophers and ask how to integrate them into a coherent history rather than treating them as decorative additions or merely assistants to famous men. This work expands the range of philosophical genres and topics, and it includes attention to women philosophers in medieval, early modern, modern, Black, and other contexts. Finally, feminist philosophers sometimes appropriate canonical thinkers, finding resources in Aristotle, Descartes, Hume, and others. The resulting interpretations can conflict, but that conflict reflects disagreements about what feminism should value and how philosophy should be practiced.
key_ideas: Feminist criticism of the canon includes studying explicit misogyny, gendered concepts, and broad patterns linking reason or objectivity with maleness.
The debate over intrinsic versus extrinsic gendering matters because it affects whether a theory can be separated from its sexist associations without being changed.
Recovering women philosophers challenges both the claim that there were no women philosophers and the claim that any women philosophers were unimportant.
Inclusion requires more than adding isolated names: historians must explain how women’s work belongs to philosophical debates and may need to broaden accepted genres and topics.
Feminist philosophers disagree about whether canonical thinkers are mainly obstacles, useful resources, or both.
These disagreements partly reflect continuing debates about feminism’s own aims, values, and self-understanding.
summaries.why_it_matters: The philosophical canon is not just a list of old authors; it shapes curricula, research questions, and the image of who belongs in philosophy. Examining exclusion can reveal how historical power influenced what counted as a philosopher, a philosophical topic, or a legitimate genre. Feminist history therefore combines historical correction with methodological criticism. It asks readers to judge arguments carefully while also examining the categories and traditions that guide judgment.

important_terms.definition: The set of philosophers, texts, and problems treated as central in a tradition or curriculum.
A reading that connects a concept, openly or through metaphor, with gender or sexual difference.
An interpretation of a tradition as a whole, rather than of only one author or passage.

A notion is intrinsically gendered if removing its gender implications would change the notion itself; it is extrinsically gendered if those implications are associated with it but are not necessary to it.
Recovering neglected thinkers and placing their work into the historical record and philosophical curriculum.
Using ideas from established philosophers as resources for current feminist questions, even when those philosophers also made sexist claims.
A project of giving proper standing to overlooked people, texts, questions, and interpretations in philosophy.

questions_to_think_about: If a philosopher’s theory is historically associated with male superiority, what would show that the association is essential rather than accidental?
Does adding women to a syllabus change the story, or can it leave the old structure untouched?
Should philosophical writing include letters, novels, religious writing, speeches, or journalism? What reasons support your answer?
Can a thinker be both an important source of sexist ideas and a useful source for feminist theory?
How might race, religion, and social position affect whose philosophical work is preserved or ignored?

summaries.example: A school reading list includes a famous philosopher but no women. A student finds a letter by Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia discussing a philosophical problem with Descartes. Simply adding her name is one kind of change. A deeper change would explain how her question belongs to the debate and how the class’s picture of philosophy changes when correspondence and questions about mind and body are included.
summaries.summary: Feminist history of philosophy studies how women and ideas about gender appear—or fail to appear—in traditional philosophical history. One task is criticism. Feminist scholars examine direct claims that women are inferior, as well as theories whose central images connect qualities such as reason, form, or objectivity with men and qualities such as matter or emotion with women. Some scholars interpret this pattern across the whole tradition; others focus on particular authors and concepts. A key disagreement is whether the gender connection is intrinsic to a theory or an added historical association. Another task is revision. Researchers recover women philosophers from different periods and ask how their work can be woven into the main story. This may require using letters, educational writing, religious texts, literature, pamphlets, and public arguments, not only standard academic treatises. The goal is not to pretend that all women philosophers were feminists or shared one style. A third task is appropriation: rereading canonical philosophers for ideas that can help feminist thinking. Thus, one philosopher may be criticized for sexist claims and still provide valuable ethical or political resources. The entry presents these disagreements as part of wider debates over feminism’s identity and over what philosophy includes.
key_ideas: Feminist philosophers criticize the canon in three main ways: by examining direct insults toward women, gendered meanings in theories, and broad links between maleness and reason or objectivity.
They debate whether gender bias is built into a theory or is an association that could be removed.
Recovering women philosophers corrects the mistaken idea that women never philosophized or that their work was unimportant.
A meaningful revision connects women’s work to philosophical debates instead of placing one woman beside an unchanged list of men.
Feminist readers sometimes disagree sharply about the same philosopher, using that philosopher either as a warning or as a resource.
The entry connects these efforts through recognition: expanding who and what philosophy recognizes.
summaries.why_it_matters: The way history is told influences who students imagine as a philosopher and which questions seem worth asking. Feminist scholarship can correct exclusions, but it also challenges the rules used to decide what counts as philosophy. It shows that recovering neglected work is not merely adding facts; it can alter the themes, methods, and boundaries of the discipline. Careful disagreement also prevents a simple division between entirely good and entirely bad thinkers.

important_terms.definition: The thinkers and books that a tradition treats as its central or most important examples.
A study of philosophy’s past that pays attention to gender, exclusion, and the treatment of women.
A claim or attitude that treats women as less capable or less valuable because they are women.
An idea that is linked with gender, either directly or through images and comparisons.
A broad interpretation that looks for a pattern across many philosophers or periods.
Changing the traditional history by recovering overlooked thinkers and reconsidering what belongs in it.
Finding useful ideas in a traditional philosopher while also recognizing that the philosopher may have held sexist views.
Giving overlooked thinkers and ideas a rightful place in the history of knowledge.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a history of philosophy leave out women even when their writings still exist?
What is the difference between adding a missing name and changing the story’s structure?
Could an idea be used in a sexist tradition without being sexist by its very nature?
Why might two feminist philosophers reach different conclusions about Aristotle or Descartes?
What kinds of writing should count as philosophy?
